concept.title: In brief
concept.shortdesc: Local service directories can be shared in a common format but still cannot be searched reliably; this work sets out to fix that.

conbody.p: Councils, charities and the NHS publish directories of local help: food banks, debt advice, lunch clubs, exercise classes, carers' groups. Open Referral UK (ORUK) is the data standard that lets those directories be shared in one common format.

The standard makes the data shareable. It does not make it findable. Each directory labels its services in its own way, or not at all. So a simple question such as “what is there near me for someone who has become unsteady on their feet?” has no reliable answer across directories.

ol.li: Work out a common way of describing services, drawn from what the listings themselves say: what each service is, what it helps with, and who it is for.
Apply that description to every listing automatically, every night, with a quoted reason for each label.
Let people and software search by meaning instead of by exact wording.

conbody.p: Recent artificial intelligence techniques do the reading and sorting. People make the decisions about the categories.
The aim is to show councils and software suppliers what can be built on ORUK data, and to give them the reusable parts. It is not to run a national service.
